newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean protest mourns death of WW2 comfort woman.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean protest mourns death of WW2 comfort woman.

text.p: South Korean activists blocked the way into the Japanese embassy in Seoul on Tuesday with a funeral ceremony to mourn the death of a woman who was forced to be a sex slave for the Japanese imperial army.

The funeral procession for Kang Duk-kyung, who died of lung cancer at the age of 68 on Sunday, stopped for one hour in front of the embassy as hundreds of activists and several former "comfort women", dressed in white traditional Korean costumes, wailed and chanted slogans.
One of the women, Yi Yong-soo, 70, braced herself against the hood of a car carrying the Japanese ambassador to Seoul, preventing him from leaving the grounds.
"Repent and compensate the comfort women," several demonstrators shouted before they piled back into buses and headed for a cemetery.
"Comfort woman" is a euphemism for women who were forced to work in Japan's frontline brothels during World War Two.

The protesters performed a play depicting the lives of the sex slaves and demanded an official apology and compensation for the victims from the Japanese government, an issue which has long troubled South Korean-Japanese relations.

In January, the controversial Asian Women's Fund, a private group set up in 1995 with Japanese government prodding, attempted to pay $42,700 each to seven Korean women, including Kang. The victims rejected the payment, calling for compensation directly from the Japanese government.
Some historians say more than 200,000 women from Korea, the Philippines, China and Indonesia were forced to become sex slaves for Japan's armed forces.

Kang, who depicted her experiences through art, was among the first group of young Korean girls taken by the Japanese military. She was raped by soldiers when she was 15 and lived for a year at a "comfort woman" camp in Japan.
Her paintings have been exhibited around South Korea to highlight the sex slave issue.
Before she was confined to bed in March, Kang participated in weekly Wednesday rallies in front of the Japanese embassy which have been staged uninterrupted since 1992.

Korea was a Japanese colony between 1910 and 1945. The two countries have been at loggerheads over various issues stemming from the period, particularly concerning compensation and an official apology from the government for war victims.
Japan has consistently argued that all war crime issues were settled when it took the legal step of signing a 1952 peace treaty in San Francisco.
